newsitem.title: USA: Florida cos. to search Bahamas reef for treasure.
newsitem.headline: Florida cos. to search Bahamas reef for treasure.

text.p: Two Florida ocean exploration companies have formed a joint venture to search for shipwrecks in a potential graveyard for treasure ships from the legendary Spanish Main, the companies announced Monday.

Tampa-based Seahawk Deep Ocean Technology Inc. and Spanish Main Treasure Co. of Tavernier will explore a 25-square-mile (64.75-square-km) area around Hogsty Reef in the southern Bahamas, company officials said.
"More than 25 wreck sites have so far been identified on Hogsty Reef," Seahawk Chief Operating Officer John Balch said.
Spanish Main secured exclusive rights from the Bahamian government to search the area until August 1998, Seahawk said in a statement.
Under the terms of the joint venture, Seahawk will be entitled to 85 percent of the gross value of recovered artifacts after the Bahamian government claimed its share, the company said.

Dozens of treasure galleons that plied the waters of the Spanish Main in the 1600s were wrecked by hurricanes and reefs in the coastal waters of Florida and the Bahamas on the return trip to Europe. The ships were also a favourite target of pirates and pirateers.

In 1985, famed Florida treasure hunter Mel Fisher hit the jackpot with the discovery of the galleon Nuestra Senora de Atocha, which was said to have yielded $400 million in gold and silver bars and coins, chains, jewelry and gemstones, in shallow waters off the Florida Keys.
Hogsty, a three-by-five mile (5-by-8 km) horseshoe-shaped reef, lies about 100 miles (160 km) north of Hispaniola, about midway between the Bahamian islands of Great Inagua and Crooked Island.
